questions.question: The chapter opens with the German proverb 'Wer Ordnung hält, ist nur zu faul zum Suchen.' What does it mean, and how does it frame the chapter?

options.text: 'If you keep tidy order, you're just too lazy to search' — order versus search
'Order is the first law of nature' — it frames the argument for normalization
'He who searches, finds' — it frames indexes as tools for searching
'Tidiness is the enemy of speed' — it frames the argument against sorting

questions.explanation: Keeping data sorted is precisely what saves you from scanning. Order versus search is the axis the whole chapter turns on, from SSTables to B-trees to column sort keys.

questions.question: 'On the most fundamental level, a database needs to do two things.' Which two?

options.text: Store data when given it, and give the data back when asked later
Enforce a declared schema, and answer queries against it
Replicate data across nodes, and tolerate node faults
Index the data for lookup, and compress it for storage

questions.explanation: Chapter 2 covered the format in which you give the database your data and the mechanism by which you ask for it again; Chapter 3 takes the database's point of view.

questions.question: Why should an application developer care how the database handles storage internally? State what the chapter concedes and what it nevertheless requires.

options.text: Concedes you won't write an engine; requires you to pick and tune one
Requires that you be able to read and modify the engine's source code
Concedes nothing; it argues every developer should write an engine once
Requires only fluency in the query language the engine exposes

questions.explanation: 'Rough idea' is the hedge, and the chapter's closing paragraphs repeat it — it aims for vocabulary, not expertise in tuning any one engine.

questions.question: Here is the chapter's world's-simplest database. Which single line is responsible for the 'most recent value' semantics? db_set appends 'key,value' to a file; db_get greps for lines starting with the key, strips the prefix with sed, and pipes through tail -n 1.

options.text: The grep, because it matches only the newest matching line in the file
The tail -n 1, because appends never overwrite, so the last match is current
The sed, because it discards the stale prefixes as it strips them
The append redirection, because it truncates the prior value first

questions.explanation: Nothing is ever overwritten; recency is recovered at read time by taking the last match. Together the two functions form a key-value store where the value may be a JSON document.

questions.question: The chapter's transcript sets key 123456 once and key 42 twice, then runs cat database. How many lines appear, and why?

options.text: Two lines, one per distinct key, since the second write replaces the first
Three lines, because both writes to key 42 survive the append
Four lines, because each overwrite also appends a tombstone record
One line, because the file is compacted the moment it is read

questions.explanation: db_set appends rather than overwriting. The storage format is roughly like a CSV file, ignoring escaping issues.

questions.question: Why does the chapter say db_set has 'pretty good performance for something that is so simple', and what does that make the file?

options.text: Appending is very efficient; the file is a log, an append-only data file
Bash is compiled ahead of time; the file is effectively a B-tree
grep is heavily optimized; the file is therefore an index
The file stays resident in memory, making it a write-through cache

questions.explanation: Many real databases use a log internally. They have more issues to deal with — concurrency control, reclaiming disk space so the log doesn't grow forever, handling errors and partially written records — but the basic principle is the same.

questions.question: A boxed note warns about the ambiguity of the word 'log'. What definition does the book adopt?

options.text: The general sense: an append-only sequence of records, perhaps binary
Strictly application logs: human-readable text describing what is happening
Strictly the write-ahead log used for crash recovery
Strictly the replication stream sent between database nodes

questions.explanation: It doesn't have to be human-readable. Getting this right matters because the book reuses 'log' in this general sense throughout, from storage engines to replication to stream processing.

questions.question: db_get is O(n). A database has 10,000 records and db_get takes 4 ms. On the chapter's model alone, roughly how long at 10 million records?

options.text: 40 ms
400 ms
4 seconds
40 seconds

questions.explanation: 10 million is 1,000 times 10,000, so 4 ms becomes 4,000 ms. At 10 billion records it is about 4,000 seconds — roughly an hour and six minutes. The chapter's gloss on O(n): double n and a lookup takes twice as long. That's not good.

questions.question: Define an index as the chapter does, and state the property that makes adding or dropping one safe.

options.text: Metadata acting as a signpost, derived from the primary data; it changes only performance
A compressed copy of the primary data, safe to drop since it regenerates
A cache of recent query results, safe to drop because entries expire
A sorted rewrite of the table, safe because the original is retained

questions.explanation: Adding and removing indexes doesn't affect the contents of the database. If you want to search the same data in several different ways, you may need several different indexes on different parts of the data.

questions.question: State 'an important trade-off in storage systems' exactly, and the policy databases adopt because of it.

options.text: Indexes speed reads but slow every write, so the developer chooses them manually
Indexes speed writes but slow reads, so databases index everything by default
Indexes are free on SSDs, so the trade-off applies only to spinning disks
Indexes cost memory but not disk, so the trade-off is purely about RAM

questions.explanation: It's hard to beat the performance of simply appending to a file, because that's the simplest possible write operation. The goal is the greatest benefit without introducing more overhead than necessary.

questions.question: Why does the chapter begin with key-value indexes, and what construct does it compare a key-value store to?

options.text: Common, and a building block for complex indexes; like a dictionary type
They are the only kind used in practice; like an array indexed by integer
They are the simplest to implement; like a singly linked list of records
Relational indexes are out of scope; like a mathematical set

questions.explanation: Dictionaries are usually implemented as hash maps — which prompts the chapter's question: since we already have hash maps for in-memory data, why not use them to index data on disk?

questions.question: Describe the simplest indexing strategy of Figure 3-1 — the write path and the read path.

options.text: An in-memory hash map of key to byte offset; append, update offset, seek
Hold the entire data file resident in memory and scan it linearly on every read
Keep a sorted on-disk index and binary search it from scratch on each read
Keep the hash map on disk and only the segment offset table in memory

questions.explanation: This works for updating existing keys too. Figure 3-1 shows storing a log of key-value pairs in a CSV-like format, indexed with an in-memory hash map.

questions.question: 'This is essentially what Bitcask does.' Which product does it belong to, and what must fit in RAM?

options.text: Riak's default engine; all keys must fit in RAM, but values may exceed it
Cassandra's default engine; both keys and values must fit in RAM
Redis's persistence layer; only the values must fit in RAM
LevelDB's index; neither keys nor values need to fit in RAM

questions.explanation: The hash map is kept completely in memory, but values can be loaded from disk with just one disk seek — and if that part of the file is already in the filesystem cache, a read needs no disk I/O at all.

questions.question: Which workload does the chapter give as a good fit for Bitcask, and which properties make it fit? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Key is a cat video's URL, value is the play count, incremented on every play
Many writes but few distinct keys, so all keys fit comfortably in memory
The value for each key is updated frequently rather than written once
Queries are predominantly range scans across sorted key ranges

questions.explanation: Range scans are exactly what a hash index cannot do efficiently — one of its two stated limitations.

questions.question: How do we avoid eventually running out of disk space, and what is compaction?

options.text: Close a segment at a size threshold; compaction keeps the newest value
Overwrite old entries in place; compaction defragments the resulting file
Delete the oldest segment periodically; compaction compresses what remains
Truncate the log on restart; compaction rebuilds the in-memory hash map

questions.explanation: Subsequent writes go to a new segment file. Figure 3-2 illustrates compaction of a key-value update log counting cat video plays.

questions.question: Why can compaction run without stopping the database? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Segments are never modified after being written, so the merge output is a new file
Merging runs in a background thread while old segments still serve requests
When the merge finishes, reads switch to the new file and old ones are deleted
Compaction takes a global write lock for only a few milliseconds at the end

questions.explanation: Since compaction often makes segments much smaller, several segments can be merged together at the same time — which is what Figure 3-3 shows.

questions.question: Once there are multiple segments, how is a key found, and what keeps this from degenerating?

options.text: Per-segment hash maps checked newest first; merging keeps the segment count small
One global hash map spans every segment, so a single lookup always suffices
All segments are searched in parallel, so their number does not matter
A Bloom filter replaces the per-segment hash maps entirely

questions.explanation: Recency ordering plus bounded segment count is what keeps this efficient.

questions.question: Which implementation issues does the chapter list as important in a real implementation? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: File format — binary with a length prefix beats CSV, and needs no escaping
Deleting records — append a tombstone so merging discards earlier values
Crash recovery — Bitcask snapshots each segment's hash map to speed restart
Checksums on every read path, so a corrupted value is repaired from a replica automatically

questions.explanation: Bitcask files do include checksums so corrupted parts are detected and ignored, but there is no automatic repair from a replica. The remaining issues are partially written records and concurrency control: writes must be strictly sequential, so there is commonly one writer thread, while immutable segments can be read concurrently. Five issues in all — most readers remember only two or three. Rebuilding hash maps by reading every segment end to end might take a long time; writes must be strictly sequential, so there is commonly one writer thread, while immutable segments can be read concurrently.

questions.question: 'An append-only log seems wasteful at first glance.' Which reasons does the chapter give in its favour? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Appending and merging are sequential writes, much faster than random ones on spinning disks
Crash recovery and concurrency are simpler when segments are immutable
Merging old segments avoids data files getting fragmented over time
Append-only logs never need compaction, since nothing is ever overwritten

questions.explanation: Note the hedge in the first reason — 'to some extent' sequential writes are also preferable on SSDs. You don't have to worry about a crash splicing part of an old and part of a new value together.

questions.question: State both limitations of a hash index. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The hash table must fit in memory; on-disk hash maps need random I/O and fiddly collision logic
Range queries are inefficient — you must look up every key individually
Hash indexes have no way to represent a deletion, so keys can never be removed
Hash indexes cannot be compacted, so their segment files grow without any bound

questions.explanation: An on-disk hash map is also expensive to grow when full. You cannot easily scan all keys between kitty00000 and kitty99999. The next section introduces a structure with neither limitation.

questions.question: What single requirement turns a log segment into an SSTable, and what is the second requirement?

options.text: Sort the pairs by key; the one-key-per-segment rule comes free from compaction
Compress each segment; the second requirement is that segments be immutable
Make all keys fixed-length; the second is that all values be fixed-length
Index every key in memory; the second is a checksum per record

questions.explanation: Sorted String Table. By default the order is the order the writes came in. At first glance sorting seems to break our ability to use sequential writes — resolved by the memtable.

questions.question: Why does merging SSTables work even when the files exceed available memory?

options.text: Mergesort style: read files side by side, copy the lowest first key, repeat
Because the files are memory-mapped and the OS handles the paging
Because each segment compresses enough to fit in available memory
Because merging reads only the in-memory indexes, never the files

questions.explanation: This produces a new merged segment file, also sorted by key. When the same key appears in several input segments, keep the value from the most recent — you can tell which is more recent because each merge takes segments from some period of time.

questions.question: With SSTables you no longer need an index of all the keys in memory. Walk the lookup of 'handiwork' when the sparse index has 'handbag' and 'handsome' but not 'handiwork'.

options.text: Jump to handbag's offset and scan forward until handiwork is found or passed
Binary search the whole segment file from its very beginning
Scan the entire segment, since the key is absent from the index
Consult a Bloom filter, which returns the exact byte offset

questions.explanation: One key for every few kilobytes of segment file is sufficient, because a few kilobytes can be scanned very quickly. A footnote notes that fixed-size keys and values would allow binary search and no in-memory index — but they are usually variable-length.

questions.question: Why does sorting make block compression natural, and what does each sparse index entry point at?

options.text: Reads scan ranges anyway, so compress records into blocks
Sorted data is inherently smaller; each entry points at a row offset
Compression requires sorted input; each entry points at a checksum
Blocks must be uniform in size; each entry points at a segment header

questions.explanation: Besides saving disk space, compression reduces I/O bandwidth use. The shaded area in Figure 3-5 is the block the index entry addresses.

questions.question: 'How do you get your data to be sorted by key in the first place? Our incoming writes can occur in any order.' What is the chapter's answer?

options.text: Keep the sorted structure in memory — a red-black or AVL tree
Re-sort the file on disk after every write completes
Require clients to submit their writes already in sorted order
Use a hash map on write and sort lazily at read time

questions.explanation: Maintaining a sorted structure on disk is possible, but in memory is much easier, and the tree reads back in sorted order. The in-memory tree is the memtable, and it is what reconciles sorted output with sequential writes.

questions.question: State the four-step LSM storage engine. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: On a write, add it to an in-memory balanced tree — the memtable
Past a size threshold of a few megabytes, flush it to disk as the newest SSTable
To read, try the memtable, then each on-disk segment from newest to oldest
Rewrite the oldest SSTable in place whenever a newer segment supersedes one of its keys

questions.explanation: Nothing is ever rewritten in place. The genuine fourth step is to run a merging and compaction process in the background from time to time, combining segment files and discarding overwritten or deleted values. Four bullets that together define the whole engine. While a memtable is being written out, writes continue to a new memtable instance.

questions.question: 'This scheme works very well. It only suffers from one problem.' Name it and the fix.

options.text: A crash loses the memtable; an unsorted append-only log on disk allows replay
Reads grow slow over time; Bloom filters skip the missing keys
The disk eventually fills up; background compaction reclaims the space
Keys arrive unsorted; a red-black tree restores the ordering

questions.explanation: Every write is immediately appended to that log; it is not sorted, but that doesn't matter because its only purpose is restoring the memtable after a crash. Each time the memtable is written out, the log can be discarded. Sortedness is unnecessary precisely because the log is replayed, never queried.

questions.question: Which facts does the chapter give about the lineage of LSM-trees? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The algorithm is what LevelDB and RocksDB use; LevelDB is a Bitcask alternative in Riak
Cassandra and HBase use similar engines, both inspired by Google's Bigtable paper
Patrick O'Neil et al. named the LSM-tree, building on log-structured filesystems
The LSM-tree was first described in Codd's 1970 paper on the relational model

questions.explanation: LevelDB and RocksDB are key-value storage engine libraries designed to be embedded into other applications. The Bigtable paper introduced the terms SSTable and memtable.

questions.question: How does Lucene reuse the SSTable idea?

options.text: Its term dictionary maps a word to a postings list in sorted files
It stores documents as SSTables while keeping its terms in a B-tree
It uses SSTables purely to cache the results of previous queries
It uses in-memory hash indexes rather than any sorted structure

questions.explanation: Lucene is the indexing engine for full-text search used by Elasticsearch and Solr; the postings list is the IDs of all documents containing the word. The full-text index mechanism is much more complex than a key-value index, but based on a similar idea.

questions.question: Which access pattern is slow on an LSM-tree, and what fixes it?

options.text: Looking up absent keys, since every segment must be checked; Bloom filters rule them out
Range scans, which sparse in-memory indexes are added to accelerate
Sequential writes, which the write-ahead log absorbs on the engine's behalf
Point lookups of keys that do exist, which compaction makes faster

questions.explanation: You check the memtable then all segments back to the oldest, possibly reading disk each time, before concluding the key doesn't exist. A Bloom filter approximates set contents and can return false positives but never false negatives — exactly the right asymmetry.

questions.question: Match the two compaction strategies to their systems and describe how each works.

options.text: Size-tiered merges small into large; leveled splits the key range by level
Size-tiered belongs to LevelDB and leveled to HBase; Cassandra supports neither of them
Both strategies are exclusive to Cassandra; LevelDB and HBase compact only on restart
Leveled merges small files into large ones; size-tiered splits the key range into levels

questions.explanation: Size-tiered is used by HBase; leveled by LevelDB (hence its name) and RocksDB; Cassandra supports both. Leveled compaction moves older data into separate levels, proceeding more incrementally and using less disk space — hence LevelDB's name. There are many subtleties, but the basic idea is simple and effective.

questions.question: Summarize the chapter's closing claims for LSM-trees.

options.text: A cascade of background-merged SSTables; works beyond memory size, ranges well, very high write throughput
Faster for reads and slower for writes than a B-tree, because segments stay sorted on disk
Requires the whole dataset to fit in available memory, which bounds its usefulness
Cannot support range queries at all, which is the price paid for write throughput

questions.explanation: Two capabilities highlighted: range queries from sortedness, and write throughput from sequentiality of the disk writes.

questions.question: How does the chapter position log-structured indexes against B-trees, and what dates does it cite?

options.text: Log-structured are gaining acceptance but B-trees dominate; introduced 1970, 'ubiquitous' within 10 years
Log-structured indexes are now the most common type; B-trees were introduced around 1980
B-trees were introduced in 1979 and were already being called ubiquitous back in 1970
The two families are equally common today, and B-trees date from roughly 1990

questions.explanation: B-trees have stood the test of time very well and remain the standard index implementation in almost all relational databases, with many nonrelational databases using them too. The 'ubiquitous' reference is Douglas Comer's 1979 survey.

questions.question: What do B-trees and SSTables share, and where do they diverge — with the unit sizes for each?

options.text: Both sort by key; log-structured uses megabyte segments, B-trees 4 KB pages
Both store fixed-size 4 KB pages, and they diverge only in how they sort the keys
Both store variable-size segments, and they diverge only in their compression scheme
Keys are unsorted in each, and the two diverge in the durability they guarantee

questions.explanation: Both allow efficient key-value lookups and range queries. Segments are written sequentially; pages are read or written one at a time, corresponding more closely to hardware, as disks are also arranged in fixed-size blocks. This is the root of every other difference.

questions.question: Define branching factor, give its value in Figure 3-6, and its typical value in practice.

options.text: Child page references per page; six in the figure; typically several hundred
The number of levels in the tree; two in the figure; typically four
Keys stored per leaf page; six in the figure; typically several thousand
The ratio of interior to leaf pages; six in the figure; typically ten

questions.explanation: In practice it depends on the space required to store page references and range boundaries. A page address is the location that lets one page refer to another — like a pointer, but on disk.

questions.question: Describe the B-tree update path and insert path.

options.text: Update changes the value in the leaf page; insert may split a full page
Both paths append the change to a log first and update the tree pages afterwards
Updates cause a page split, whereas inserts simply overwrite the existing page in place
Both paths require rewriting the root page in order to record the new tree version

questions.explanation: References to an updated page remain valid. On a split, two half-full pages result and the parent is updated to reflect the new subdivision of key ranges. Figure 3-7 shows this. A footnote notes deletion while keeping the tree balanced is more involved.

questions.question: A four-level tree of 4 KB pages with a branching factor of 500 can store up to how much, and what is the typical depth?

options.text: 256 TB, and most databases are three or four levels deep
256 GB, with a typical depth of six or seven levels
2.56 PB, with a typical depth of only two levels
25.6 TB, with a typical depth of about ten levels

questions.explanation: 500 to the fourth power is 62,500,000,000 pages, times 4 KB is about 2.56 times 10 to the 14th bytes. The algorithm keeps the tree balanced, so depth is O(log n) — you don't need to follow many page references.

questions.question: State the B-tree's fundamental write operation and the assumption it rests on.

options.text: Overwrite the page in place, its location unchanged so references hold
Append the new page and then update the parent's pointer to it
Write the page to a fresh location and garbage-collect the old copy
Buffer the change in memory and flush it only at commit time

questions.explanation: This is in stark contrast to log-structured indexes, which only append and never modify files in place. On a magnetic drive it means moving the head, waiting for the platter position, and overwriting the sector; on SSDs it is more complicated, since large blocks must be erased and rewritten.

questions.question: Why can a single logical insert require several page overwrites, and what structure fixes the resulting danger?

options.text: A split writes both halves and the parent; the WAL is written first
Because pages are compressed on write; per-page checksums detect the damage
Because the root must be rewritten each time; copy-on-write avoids the risk
Because leaves are chained together; sibling pointers repair the chain

questions.explanation: You could end up with an orphan page that is not a child of any parent. The write-ahead log (also called a redo log) is an append-only file every modification must be written to before being applied to the tree, and is replayed after a crash. Crucially, the WAL is written before the pages, not after.

questions.question: What concurrency problem does update-in-place create, and why are log-structured approaches simpler here?

options.text: Threads could see an inconsistent tree, so latches guard it
B-trees need distributed consensus, which log-structured engines avoid
B-trees demand serializable transactions; log-structured engines are single-threaded
Log-structured engines need latches too, making them equally complex

questions.explanation: Log-structured engines merge in the background without interfering with queries, then atomically swap old segments for new. Latches are lightweight locks. Log-structured engines do all the merging in the background without interfering with incoming queries, then atomically swap old segments for new. Immutability is what removes the need for reader-writer coordination.

questions.question: Which B-tree optimizations does the chapter list? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Copy-on-write — write the modified page elsewhere and create new parent versions (LMDB)
Abbreviated keys — interior pages need only boundaries, so more keys fit per page
Sequential leaf layout and sibling pointers, to scan in order without revisiting parents
Bloom filters on every interior page, so a lookup can skip levels that cannot hold the key

questions.explanation: Bloom filters belong to LSM-trees, not to B-tree interior pages. The fourth optimization the chapter names is fractal trees, variants that borrow log-structured ideas to reduce disk seeks — and which have nothing to do with fractals. Five optimizations, 'to mention just a few'. Copy-on-write replaces the WAL for crash recovery. Sequential leaf layout is hard to maintain as the tree grows; by contrast LSM-trees rewrite large segments in one go, making it easier to keep sequential keys close together.

questions.question: Explain the causal chain from abbreviating interior-page keys to fewer disk reads.

options.text: Shorter keys, more per page, higher branching factor, fewer levels, fewer page reads
Shorter keys compress better, so each page loads from disk faster
Shorter keys reduce the time a latch is held, cutting contention
Shorter keys leave room to inline the sibling pointers in each page

questions.explanation: The whole chain rests on the fixed page size: space saved on keys converts directly into branching factor, and B-trees read or write one page at a time.

questions.question: True or false, per the chapter: a B-tree page's location changes when it is overwritten; the WAL must be written after the tree pages are updated; fractal trees are named for their self-similar geometry.

options.text: All three are false
All three are true
Only the first is false
Only the third is false

questions.explanation: The overwrite is assumed not to change the page's location, the WAL must be written before the pages, and fractal trees have nothing to do with fractals. The chapter does state as true that 4 KB is the traditional page size and pages may be bigger.

questions.question: State the rule of thumb comparing LSM-trees and B-trees, and note the hedge.

options.text: LSM faster for writes, B-trees 'thought to be' faster for reads
LSM-trees are faster for both reads and writes, with no hedge attached
B-trees are definitively faster for reads, as benchmarks consistently show
The two are indistinguishable in practice on modern hardware

questions.explanation: The hedged verb matters, because reads are typically slower on LSM-trees as they check several structures and SSTables at different stages of compaction. Benchmarks are sensitive to workload details, so test with your own. B-tree implementations are also generally more mature, which confounds the comparison.

questions.question: Define write amplification, and state how many times a B-tree writes each piece of data at minimum.

options.text: One write causing several disk writes; a B-tree writes at least twice
The ratio of index size to data size; a B-tree writes each datum once
The growth of the log over time; a B-tree writes each datum three times
Pages touched per query; a B-tree writes each datum four times

questions.explanation: And perhaps again as pages are split. There's also overhead from writing an entire page even if a few bytes changed, and some engines overwrite the same page twice to avoid a partially updated page on power failure. Log-structured indexes also rewrite data multiple times due to compaction.

questions.question: Which two distinct costs of write amplification does the chapter name? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Hardware wear, since SSD blocks tolerate only a limited number of overwrites
Throughput, since more disk writes mean fewer writes per second within the bandwidth
Increased read latency caused by growing file fragmentation
Higher memory consumption for the engine's write buffer

questions.explanation: One cost is to the device, the other to the workload. In write-heavy applications the bottleneck might be the rate at which the database can write to disk.

questions.question: Give both reasons LSM-trees sustain higher write throughput, including the hedge on the first.

options.text: Sometimes lower write amplification, and sequential rather than page writes
They always have strictly lower write amplification and never need a write-ahead log at all
They hold all recent data in memory and write it out to disk purely asynchronously
They compress data more effectively and skip the background merge step altogether

questions.explanation: The explicit hedge on write amplification is the chapter being careful not to overclaim. The difference is particularly important on magnetic hard drives, where sequential writes are much faster than random writes.

questions.question: Why do LSM-trees produce smaller files, where does a B-tree lose space, and what does SSD firmware do that partly neutralizes the argument?

options.text: Better compression; B-trees fragment pages; SSD firmware blunts only part
B-trees compress better; LSM-trees lose space to overlapping segments; firmware erases the gap
Neither compresses meaningfully; the difference is purely in seek behaviour
LSM-trees waste space on tombstones, which the SSD firmware reclaims for them

questions.explanation: The firmware turns random writes into sequential ones, so the write-pattern edge shrinks, but the compactness advantage remains. When a B-tree page splits, or a row cannot fit an existing page, space is left unused. LSM-trees are not page-oriented and periodically rewrite SSTables, so overheads are lower, especially with leveled compaction. Firmware turns random writes into sequential ones — but compactness still allows more requests within the available I/O bandwidth.

questions.question: State the first downside of log-structured storage, and where the damage shows up.

options.text: Compaction competes with live traffic; high percentiles suffer most
Compaction can corrupt data, which is why checksums are required
Compaction requires taking the database offline periodically
Compaction raises average response time sharply while leaving percentiles flat

questions.explanation: Engines try to compact incrementally, but disks have limited resources, so a request may wait for an expensive compaction to finish — and B-trees can be more predictable. The chapter cross-references Describing Performance: the tail-latency argument from Chapter 1 applied to storage.

questions.question: Describe the failure mode when compaction can't keep up at high write throughput.

options.text: Segments pile up until the disk fills; engines don't throttle, so monitor
The database automatically throttles incoming writes, so nothing actually breaks down
Compaction is given scheduling priority and the incoming writes start failing with errors
Reads get faster, because fewer merge operations are competing for the disk bandwidth

questions.explanation: Finite write bandwidth is shared between the initial write — logging and flushing a memtable — and background compaction, and the bigger the database the more bandwidth compaction needs. The absence of back-pressure makes this an operational duty rather than a self-correcting condition.

questions.question: Give the B-tree advantage that has nothing to do with speed.

options.text: Each key exists in exactly one place, so range locks can attach directly to the tree
B-trees have no need for a write-ahead log, since pages are overwritten atomically
B-trees can be compressed considerably more aggressively than sorted segment files
B-trees support efficient range queries, which LSM-trees are unable to provide

questions.explanation: A log-structured engine may have multiple copies of the same key in different segments. This makes B-trees attractive where strong transactional semantics are wanted: in many relational databases isolation is implemented using locks on key ranges. Uniqueness of location is what makes such a lock well-defined.

questions.question: Summarize the section's closing judgment on B-trees versus LSM-trees.

options.text: B-trees are ingrained and staying; log-structured is rising; test it
LSM-trees are the clear winner and B-trees are now legacy technology
B-trees win across every workload the chapter considers
The chapter supplies a decision table that settles the question

questions.explanation: B-trees provide consistently good performance for many workloads. There is no quick and easy rule for determining which type is better for your use case — the chapter predicts, concedes, then explicitly refuses to give a rule.

questions.question: Key-value indexes are analogous to what, and what does a primary key uniquely identify in each of the three data models?

options.text: A primary key index: one row, one document, or one vertex
A secondary index: one column in each of the three models
A clustered index: one page in each of the three models
A covering index: one partition in each of the three models

questions.explanation: Other records can refer to that row, document or vertex by its primary key or ID, and the index is used to resolve such references.

questions.question: How are secondary indexes created in relational databases, and why are they crucial?

options.text: With CREATE INDEX; they are crucial for performing joins efficiently
Automatically by the optimizer; they are crucial for durability
With ALTER TABLE; they are crucial for enforcing uniqueness constraints
They cannot be added after the table has been created

questions.explanation: For example the user_id columns in the Figure 2-1 example from Chapter 2, used to find all rows belonging to the same user. Joins are the workload that makes secondary indexes non-optional.

questions.question: A secondary index can easily be constructed from a key-value index. What is the main difference, and what are the two ways to solve it?

options.text: Keys are not unique; store a list of row IDs per key, or append a row ID to the key
They cannot be sorted; solved by hashing or by partitioning the index
They cannot be updated; solved by rebuilding or by versioning entries
They must be clustered; solved by covering columns or by interleaving

questions.explanation: A list of matching row identifiers is like a postings list in a full-text index. Either way, both B-trees and log-structured indexes can be used — non-uniqueness is the only structural difference, and the index type is orthogonal to it.

questions.question: Define a heap file and describe what happens when an updated value grows too large to overwrite in place.

options.text: An unordered row store behind the indexes; a grown row moves elsewhere
A file kept sorted by primary key; a value that grows too large is compressed to fit the page
An in-memory structure holding hot rows; oversized values are spilled out to disk
The write-ahead log itself; an oversized value is split across several tree pages

questions.explanation: If the new value is larger, the row probably moves to a new heap location, and then either every index is updated or a forwarding pointer is left behind. An index value can be the actual row or a reference to it. A heap file may be append-only, or may track deleted rows to overwrite later, and avoids duplicating data when multiple secondary indexes exist. The forwarding pointer is the cheaper option, at the cost of an extra hop on read.

questions.question: Define a clustered index and give the chapter's two concrete product behaviours.

options.text: It stores the row inside the index itself
It groups rows by partition key; InnoDB and SQL Server both allow many per table
It is another name for a covering index, which InnoDB forbids
It sorts the heap file; SQL Server maintains one automatically per column

questions.explanation: In MySQL's InnoDB the primary key is always a clustered index and secondary indexes refer to it; in SQL Server you can specify one clustered index per table. It is used when the extra hop from index to heap file is too much of a read penalty. In InnoDB, secondary indexes refer to the primary key rather than a heap file location.

questions.question: What sits between a clustered and a nonclustered index, and what is the phrase for when it succeeds?

options.text: A covering index, storing some columns; it is said to cover the query
A partial index, storing some rows; it is said to satisfy the query
A concatenated index, combining columns; it is said to span the query
A sparse index, storing some keys; it is said to short-circuit the query

questions.explanation: Also called an index with included columns. It allows some queries to be answered from the index alone. A clustered index stores all row data within the index; a nonclustered index stores only references.

questions.question: Clustered and covering indexes speed up reads. Which costs does the chapter attach? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: They require additional storage space
They can add overhead on writes
The database must work harder so duplication never shows as inconsistency
They make range queries unusable on the indexed columns

questions.explanation: Any kind of duplication of data carries these three costs, the third being about transactional guarantees.

questions.question: Define a concatenated index, give the chapter's analogy, and state which query shapes work.

options.text: Fields appended into one key, like a phone book on (lastname, firstname)
Each column indexed separately; all three query shapes work equally well
The columns hashed together; only exact full-key matches can be served
Sorted by the last column first; first-name queries work, last-name queries fail

questions.explanation: So you can query by last name, or last plus first name — but not by first name alone. The index definition specifies in which order the fields are concatenated. Order is everything: prefix queries work, suffix queries don't. A one-column index is not sufficient when you need to query multiple columns simultaneously.

questions.question: A restaurant search filters latitude within a narrow band AND longitude within a narrow band. Why can't a standard B-tree or LSM-tree answer it efficiently?

options.text: Two range predicates at once; one range is served, the other unbounded
Because floating-point coordinates cannot be indexed at all
Because the predicates are combined with AND rather than OR
Because latitude and longitude live in separate tables

questions.explanation: You get all restaurants in a latitude range at any longitude, or all in a longitude range anywhere between the poles, but not both simultaneously. This is where a concatenated index falls short and multi-dimensional indexes earn their place.

questions.question: How are multi-dimensional indexes actually built, and what stack does PostGIS use?

options.text: A space-filling curve into a B-tree, or more often a specialized R-tree
Only space-filling curves are used in practice; PostGIS builds a B-tree over a Hilbert curve
Only quadtrees are used for this; PostGIS ships a dedicated quadtree index extension
Multi-dimensional indexes remain theoretical and are not implemented in real databases

questions.explanation: PostGIS implements geospatial indexes as R-trees using PostgreSQL's Generalized Search Tree (GiST) facility. GiST is the Generalized Search Tree indexing facility. The chapter says it doesn't have space to describe R-trees in detail, but there is plenty of literature on them.

questions.question: Which non-geographic multi-dimensional index examples does the chapter give, and what would a one-dimensional index force you to do for the weather query? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Ecommerce — a three-dimensional index on (red, green, blue) to search colour ranges
Weather — a two-dimensional index on (date, temperature) for 2013 at 25-30 degrees
One dimension forces scanning all of 2013 then filtering, or vice versa; HyperDex does 2D
Genomics — a four-dimensional index over nucleotide positions

questions.explanation: A 2D index could narrow down by timestamp and temperature simultaneously. An interesting idea is that multi-dimensional indexes are not just for geographic locations.

questions.question: What shared assumption do all the indexes so far make, and what specific capabilities do full-text search engines add?

options.text: They assume exact data; search engines add synonyms, grammatical variants, proximity and edit distance
They assume the data is already sorted; search engines add compression of the index itself
They assume every key is unique; search engines relax this to allow duplicate keys
They assume numeric keys throughout; search engines extend the idea to string keys

questions.explanation: They query exact values of a key, or a range with a sort order — they don't find similar keys such as misspelled words. Lucene searches within a certain edit distance, where 1 means one letter added, removed, or replaced. Exactness is the shared assumption; fuzziness needs a different structure.

questions.question: How does Lucene's in-memory index differ from LevelDB's, and what transformation does Lucene apply?

options.text: LevelDB keeps sparse keys; Lucene a trie-like finite state automaton
Lucene keeps a sparse collection of keys while LevelDB keeps a trie over key characters
Lucene keeps no in-memory index at all, whereas LevelDB indexes every key it stores
Both keep Bloom filters in memory, differing only in how much space they allocate

questions.explanation: That automaton can be transformed into a Levenshtein automaton, which supports efficient search within a given edit distance. Both keep a small in-memory index telling queries at which offset in the sorted file to look. The Levenshtein automaton supports efficient search within a given edit distance. Other fuzzy techniques go toward document classification and machine learning.

questions.question: State the chapter's complaint about disks and the two advantages that make us tolerate them — and which one is eroding.

options.text: Awkward layout demands; durable and cheaper per gigabyte, cost edge eroding
Slow access; capacity and reliability, with reliability eroding over time
High price; speed and durability, with the speed advantage eroding
Physical fragility; cost and portability, with portability eroding

questions.explanation: Both magnetic disks and SSDs need data laid out carefully for good performance. Durable means contents survive a power cut. Many datasets are simply not that big, so keeping them entirely in memory becomes feasible, potentially across several machines — hence in-memory databases.

questions.question: Contrast Memcached with in-memory databases that aim for durability, listing the durability mechanisms. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Memcached is for caching only, where losing data on restart is acceptable
Special hardware such as battery-powered RAM, or writing a change log to disk
Writing periodic snapshots to disk, or replicating in-memory state to other machines
An in-memory database forfeits durability by definition, which is why Memcached is typical

questions.explanation: When an in-memory database is restarted it needs to reload its state, either from disk or over the network from a replica — unless special hardware is used.

questions.question: An in-memory database may write to disk. Why is it still called in-memory?

options.text: The disk is only an append-only durability log; all reads are served from memory
Because the writes to disk happen asynchronously in the background
Because the disk holds only the index, never the data itself
Because the disk file is memory-mapped rather than read normally

questions.explanation: The read path, not the write path, defines the category. The disk file also has the operational advantage that it can easily be backed up, inspected, and analyzed by external utilities.

questions.question: Match the in-memory products to what the chapter says about them.

options.text: VoltDB, MemSQL and TimesTen are relational; RAMCloud is durable key-value
Redis and Couchbase are relational; VoltDB and MemSQL are strongly durable key-value stores
RAMCloud is relational; TimesTen is a cache with no durability at all
All six achieve strong durability through battery-backed RAM

questions.explanation: Redis and Couchbase provide only weak durability, writing to disk asynchronously. The relational vendors claim big performance improvements from removing on-disk data structure overheads — the chapter reports the claim rather than endorsing it. RAMCloud is open source and uses a log-structured approach in memory as well as on disk; Redis and Couchbase write to disk asynchronously.

questions.question: Why are in-memory databases fast? Give the reason most people assume and the real one.

options.text: Not avoided disk reads — the OS caches those — but avoided serialization
Simply that RAM has far lower latency than disk, which is the whole story
Because they can skip maintaining a write-ahead log at all
Because they use vectorized processing over compressed columns

questions.explanation: Counterintuitively, even a disk-based engine may never read from disk given enough memory, because the OS caches recently used blocks. Serialization overhead, not I/O, is the real cost being avoided.

questions.question: Besides performance, what does the chapter call 'another interesting area' for in-memory databases?

options.text: Data models awkward on disk, as Redis does with queues and sets
Transactional guarantees stronger than any disk-based system offers
Replication being built in rather than bolted on afterwards
Schema-on-read flexibility that disk engines cannot provide

questions.explanation: Because it keeps all data in memory, Redis's implementation is comparatively simple. Keeping everything in memory makes exotic data structures cheap to implement.

questions.question: Describe the anti-caching approach and the limitation it still has.

options.text: Evict least-recently-used records at record granularity, beating OS paging
Compress the cold records in place; the whole dataset must still fit inside memory
Replicate cold records to other machines; access patterns must stay uniform across keys
It behaves exactly like operating system swapping, so it offers no advantage and needs no index

questions.explanation: It still requires indexes to fit entirely in memory, like the Bitcask example at the start of the chapter. It loads data back when accessed again — similar to OS virtual memory and swap, but the database works at the granularity of individual records rather than whole memory pages. The in-memory index requirement is the same one Bitcask had at the start of the chapter.

questions.question: What technology does the chapter say may force further storage engine redesign, and how confidently?

options.text: Non-volatile memory; changes 'probably' needed, still a research area
Quantum storage, which it says will certainly force a redesign
Shingled magnetic recording, which it says has already forced one
Persistent GPU memory, which it explicitly dismisses

questions.explanation: Deliberately hedged — 'probably', 'new area of research', 'worth keeping an eye on'.

questions.question: Where does the word 'transaction' come from, and what is the modern definition?

options.text: Commercial transactions in business data processing; now any group of reads and writes forming a logical unit
Double-entry bookkeeping in accounting; it now means a single write applied atomically
Telephone exchange switching terminology; it now means one request and its response
The ACID literature of the 1980s; it now means any operation running in full isolation

questions.explanation: A write typically corresponded to making a sale, placing an order with a supplier, or paying a salary. As databases expanded into areas without money changing hands the term nevertheless stuck — a useful reminder that the word carries no technical guarantee by itself.

questions.question: A boxed note makes a careful disclaimer about ACID. What does it deny and what does it assert?

options.text: Denies that transactions must be ACID; asserts the term just means low-latency reads and writes
Asserts that every transaction is ACID by the very definition of the word transaction
Denies that batch processing is a meaningful category distinct from transaction processing
Asserts that ACID properties are required for OLTP systems but never for OLAP ones

questions.explanation: As opposed to batch processing jobs, which only run periodically, for example once per day. Forward references: ACID properties in Chapter 7, batch processing in Chapter 10.

questions.question: Describe the OLTP access pattern and expand the acronym.

options.text: A few records fetched by key via an index; online transaction processing
Many records scanned and aggregated per query; online table processing
Bulk writes applied once per day in a window; offline transaction processing
Whole tables read into memory and joined; optimized lookup transaction processing

questions.explanation: Because these applications are interactive, the access pattern became known as OLTP. Even as databases came to hold blog comments, game actions and address books, the basic pattern remained similar to processing business transactions.

questions.question: Describe the analytic access pattern and its example queries. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Scan a huge number of records, read a few columns each, and compute aggregates
What was each store's total revenue in January? How many extra bananas sold during the promotion?
Which brand of baby food is most often bought together with brand X diapers?
What is the current balance of account 12345, as of the most recent posted entry?

questions.explanation: The last one is an OLTP query. Aggregates such as count, sum or average are returned rather than the raw data. Analytic queries are often written by business analysts and feed reports that help management decide — business intelligence.

questions.question: Expand OLAP and state the hedge the chapter makes about the OLTP/OLAP distinction.

options.text: Online analytic processing; the difference is not always clear-cut
Offline analytic processing; the distinction from OLTP is absolute and never blurred
Optimized aggregate processing; the distinction concerns data volume and nothing else
Online aggregate protocol; the distinction is entirely a matter of vendor marketing

questions.explanation: A footnote notes the meaning of 'online' in OLAP is unclear; it probably refers to queries not being just predefined reports — analysts use the system interactively for explorative queries. Note the double hedge: 'unclear' and 'probably'.

questions.question: In Table 3-1, which dataset sizes does the chapter give for OLTP and OLAP?

options.text: Gigabytes to terabytes for OLTP; terabytes to petabytes for OLAP
Megabytes to gigabytes for OLTP; gigabytes to terabytes for OLAP
Terabytes to petabytes for OLTP; gigabytes to terabytes for OLAP
Gigabytes to terabytes for both OLTP and OLAP

questions.explanation: The table compares five properties: main read pattern, main write pattern (random-access low-latency writes from user input versus bulk import via ETL or an event stream), who primarily uses it (end user versus internal analyst), what the data represents (latest state versus history of events), and dataset size.

questions.question: When did analytics move out of OLTP databases, and what was the separate database called?

options.text: Late 1980s and early 1990s, into a data warehouse
Late 1990s, into what was then called a data lake
The 1970s, into a decision support system
The 2000s, into what is now called a lakehouse

questions.explanation: At first the same databases were used for both, since SQL turned out to be quite flexible in this regard.

questions.question: State the two expectations placed on OLTP systems and the harm an ad hoc analytic query does.

options.text: High availability and low latency; ad hoc scans contend with concurrent transactions
Durability and consistency; ad hoc queries can corrupt stored data
Scalability and low cost; ad hoc queries exhaust available disk space
Schema flexibility; ad hoc queries invalidate the existing schema

questions.explanation: They are often critical to the operation of the business, so administrators closely guard them and are reluctant to let analysts run expensive queries that scan large parts of the dataset. Resource contention with latency-critical transactions is the specific harm.

questions.question: Define a data warehouse and expand ETL, listing the stages of getting data in.

options.text: A read-only copy of all OLTP data for unrestricted querying; Extract-Transform-Load
A write-optimized replica of the OLTP database; Extract-Transfer-Log
A cache of the reports analysts run most often; Evaluate-Transform-Load
A distributed filesystem holding raw files; Export-Translate-Load

questions.explanation: Analysts can query it to their hearts' content without affecting OLTP operations. Data is extracted by periodic dump or continuous stream, transformed into an analysis-friendly schema, cleaned up, then loaded. Figure 3-8 outlines this.

questions.question: Why are data warehouses almost unheard of in small companies? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: They probably don't have many different OLTP systems to integrate
Their data is small enough for a conventional SQL database or a spreadsheet
Warehouse software is not made available to smaller companies
Small companies do not run analytics of any kind

questions.explanation: The chapter closes with the aphorism: in a large company, a lot of heavy lifting is required to do something that is simple in a small company.

questions.question: What is the 'big advantage' of a separate warehouse, and what does the chapter admit about the first half of the chapter?

options.text: It can be optimized for analytics; the OLTP indexing just covered won't do
The advantage is lower cost; the first half applies equally to analytics
The advantage is durability; the first half was about analytics all along
The advantage is schema flexibility; the first half is entirely superseded

questions.explanation: So the rest of the chapter looks at storage engines optimized for analytics instead — an unusually direct admission that the preceding forty pages don't transfer.

questions.question: What data model do warehouses commonly use and why, and what looks alike versus different?

options.text: Relational, as SQL suits analytics; same SQL surface as OLTP but very different internals
Document-oriented, because analytics data arrives deeply nested from source systems
Graph-oriented, because warehouse dimensions are richly interconnected with each other
Key-value, because analytic queries almost always look rows up by their primary key

questions.explanation: Graphical tools generate SQL, visualize results, and allow drill-down and slicing and dicing. The internals are optimized for very different query patterns, which is why many vendors now focus on either transaction processing or analytics, but not both.

questions.question: What does the chapter say about vendors, RedShift, and SQL-on-Hadoop? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: SQL Server and SAP HANA support both, but increasingly as two engines behind one SQL interface
The market is dominated by expensive licences — Teradata, Vertica, SAP HANA, ParAccel; RedShift hosts ParAccel
Open source SQL-on-Hadoop has proliferated: Hive, Spark SQL, Impala, Presto, Tajo, Drill
Every data warehouse product on the market is open source and free of any licence cost

questions.explanation: The SQL-on-Hadoop projects are young but aim to compete with commercial warehouses, some based on ideas from Google's Dremel. A snapshot of a market splitting along the OLTP/OLAP line.

questions.question: Contrast the variety of data models in transactional and analytic worlds, and give both names for the analytic style.

options.text: Far less diversity, being formulaic: star schema, or dimensional modeling
Analytics has more model diversity; the style is called normalized modeling
Both worlds use only relational models; the style is called cube modeling
Analytics uses graph models; the style is called network modeling

questions.explanation: Chapter 2 described a wide range of transactional models. Formulaic is the operative word — the shape is highly conventional.

questions.question: What sits at the centre of a star schema, and what does one row mean?

options.text: A fact table such as fact_sales; each row is one event
A dimension table; each row represents one business entity
A summary table; each row holds one precomputed aggregate
A date table; each row represents a single calendar day

questions.explanation: In Figure 3-9's grocery retailer example. For website traffic instead, each row would represent a page view or a click by a user.

questions.question: Why do fact tables get enormous, and what scale does the chapter cite?

options.text: Events are stored individually rather than pre-aggregated; Apple, Walmart or eBay hold tens of petabytes
Facts are duplicated once per dimension they reference; the cited scale is a few terabytes
Facts are never deleted once written; the cited scale is exabytes in Google's warehouse
Facts inline every dimension attribute they need; the cited scale is tens of gigabytes

questions.explanation: Individual events allow maximum flexibility of analysis later, at the cost of an extremely large table running to trillions of rows. Dimension tables are usually much smaller — millions of rows — which is why the chapter concentrates on storage of facts.

questions.question: Distinguish the two kinds of columns in a fact table, and give the mnemonic for what dimensions represent.

options.text: Attribute columns plus foreign keys to dimensions; who, what, where, when
Some columns are keys and others precomputed aggregates; dimensions give the how much
Some columns are measures and others timestamps; dimensions give the ordering of events
Every column is a foreign key reference; the dimensions record the schema version used

questions.explanation: The attributes include the price at which the product sold and the cost of buying it from the supplier, allowing the profit margin to be calculated; the dimensions represent the who, what, where, when, how and why of the event. Price sold and supplier cost allow the profit margin to be calculated. The who/what/where/when/how/why mnemonic is the chapter's own.

questions.question: What does a dim_product row contain, and why do even dates get a dimension table?

options.text: One product type, with SKU, brand, category and package size
One sale line item; dates get their own dimension table purely in order to save space
One supplier of the product; dates get a dimension table to handle time zone conversion
One product category; dates are instead stored inline as columns on the fact table

questions.explanation: Even date and time get dimension tables, because that allows extra information such as public holidays to be encoded, so queries can separate holiday from non-holiday sales. Encoding public holidays lets queries differentiate between sales on holidays and non-holidays. Each fact_sales row uses a foreign key to indicate which product was sold; several products bought at once are represented as separate rows.

questions.question: Explain the name 'star schema', define the snowflake variant, and say which is usually preferred.

options.text: The fact table sits centrally, ringed by dimensions like a star's rays
Named after a star-shaped index structure; snowflake is always preferred for normalization
Named for the fan-out pattern of its queries; the two variants are exactly equivalent
Named for its five surrounding dimensions; snowflake simply means fully denormalized

questions.explanation: In the snowflake variant dimensions are broken into subdimensions — separate tables for brands and categories — which is more normalized, but star schemas are preferred as they are simpler for analysts. Like the rays of a star. Snowflake breaks dimensions into subdimensions — separate tables for brands and categories, referenced by foreign key rather than stored as strings — and is more normalized. Analyst ergonomics beats normalization purity here.

questions.question: How wide are warehouse tables, and what fraction of a fact table row does a typical query actually need?

options.text: Often over 100 columns, sometimes several hundred; a query touches 4 or 5, discarding 95% or more
About ten columns in total, and a typical analytic query reads most of them
Several thousand columns, of which a typical query reads roughly half at a time
About a hundred columns, of which a typical query genuinely needs around eighty

questions.explanation: SELECT-star queries are rarely needed for analytics. Dimension tables are wide too: dim_store carries which services each store offers, whether it has an in-store bakery, square footage, opening date, last remodel, and distance to the nearest highway.

questions.question: Describe row-oriented storage and explain why an index on date_key or product_sk still leaves an analytic query slow.

options.text: Whole rows sit contiguously, so 100+ attributes load just to read five
Because the index is not kept sorted, which forces a full table scan regardless
Because an index cannot be combined with a GROUP BY clause in the same query
Because the index covers only the dimension tables and never the fact table

questions.explanation: Document databases are similar, storing a whole document as one contiguous byte sequence. The index tells the engine where the rows are, but it still loads them all, parses them, and filters. The index solves row location, not row width — the whole motivation for columnar storage.

questions.question: State the column-oriented idea in the chapter's own words.

options.text: Store all values of each column together, so reads touch only those used
Store each row twice over, once in sorted order and once in insertion order
Keep every column resident in memory while the rows themselves stay on disk
Store only those columns that already carry a secondary index on them

questions.explanation: Don't store all the values from one row together. If each column is in a separate file, a query only reads and parses the columns it needs, which can save a lot of work. Figure 3-10 shows this.

questions.question: A boxed note guards against a misreading of column storage. What does it say, and what does Parquet demonstrate?

options.text: It applies to nonrelational data too, as Parquet does for documents
It works only with relational models; Parquet is the exception proving the rule
It demands a fixed schema; Parquet enforces one strictly
Column storage is a data model, not a layout; Parquet is a data model

questions.explanation: Parquet is a columnar format supporting a document data model, based on Google's Dremel. Columnar storage is a physical layout choice, independent of the logical model. Columnar storage is a physical layout choice, independent of the logical data model — the distinction being protected.

questions.question: State the one invariant column-oriented storage relies on.

options.text: Every column file holds rows in the same order, so the 23rd entry of each forms row 23
Every column file is sorted independently according to its own values
Every column file must occupy exactly the same number of bytes on disk
Every column file carries its own copy of the table's primary key column

questions.explanation: Positional correspondence is also what makes bitwise AND across bitmaps valid: the kth bit in one column's bitmap corresponds to the same row as the kth bit in another's.

questions.question: Why does column data compress well, and which technique does the chapter single out for data warehouses?

options.text: The values in a column are often repetitive; bitmap encoding is singled out
Column data is always numeric; delta encoding is singled out
Column data is sorted by definition; dictionary encoding is singled out
Column data is small in volume; plain gzip is singled out

questions.explanation: Which is a good sign for compression, and different techniques suit different data. Figure 3-11 shows compressed, bitmap-indexed storage of a single column. Besides loading fewer columns, compression further reduces demands on disk throughput.

questions.question: Define bitmap encoding precisely, and explain what is done when the bitmaps are sparse.

options.text: One bitmap per distinct value, one bit per row; sparse ones are run-length encoded
One bitmap per row with one bit per distinct value; sparse bitmaps are discarded
A hash of each value per row; sparse values fall back to plain strings
A sorted list of the distinct values; sparse columns are left unencoded

questions.explanation: The bit is 1 if the row has that value. This works because distinct values are often few compared to rows. For a product_sk column over a billion rows with 100,000 products, raw bitmaps would be 10 to the 14th bits — about 12.5 TB — hence run-length encoding. A country column may have about 200 distinct values and needs one bit per row.

questions.question: A query filters product_sk to one of three values; another filters product_sk = 31 AND store_sk = 3. What bitwise operations do these become?

options.text: A bitwise OR of three bitmaps, then a bitwise AND of two; valid because column files share row order
An AND of three bitmaps then an OR of two; validity comes from each column being sorted
Both become XOR operations over the bitmaps; validity comes from the stored checksums
Bitmap columns cannot be combined at all, so each predicate is evaluated as a separate scan

questions.explanation: The OR can be done very efficiently. The kth bit in one column's bitmap corresponds to the same row as the kth bit in another's. Bitmap indexes are very well suited to the kinds of queries common in a data warehouse.

questions.question: A boxed note calls a common description of Cassandra and HBase 'very misleading'. Which description, and why?

options.text: Calling Bigtable-style column families columnar; a row's columns sit together
Calling them row-oriented, when internally they are in fact a true columnar layout
Calling them key-value stores, when their data model is really a relational one
Calling them LSM-based engines, when they actually store their data in B-trees

questions.explanation: They also do not use column compression, so the Bigtable model is still mostly row-oriented. Within each column family they store all columns from a row together, along with a row key, so the Bigtable model is still mostly row-oriented. A widely repeated mislabel the chapter takes care to correct.

questions.question: Disk-to-memory bandwidth is a big bottleneck but not the only one. Which others do developers of analytical databases worry about? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Using the bandwidth from main memory into the CPU cache efficiently
Avoiding branch mispredictions and bubbles in the CPU pipeline
Making use of single-instruction-multi-data instructions in modern CPUs
Reducing the number of network round-trips to the storage layer

questions.explanation: The performance story moves from disk down into the CPU.

questions.question: Define vectorized processing and explain how columnar layout helps the CPU.

options.text: Loop over an L1-resident chunk, operating on the compressed form directly
Use GPUs rather than CPUs for the aggregation work, since GPUs have wider registers
Decompress each column block first, then process the resulting rows one at a time
Spread every query across many machines so each handles a slice of the columns

questions.explanation: No function calls per record, unlike code needing calls and conditions for each. Column compression lets more rows fit in the same L1 cache. The key point: operators such as the bitwise AND and OR work on the compressed representation without decompressing first.

questions.question: What order is easiest in a column store, and what does imposing an order buy you?

options.text: Insertion order, since inserting just appends; an imposed order indexes it
Sorted order is easiest; imposing insertion order is what enables compression
Random order is easiest; imposing an order is what enables replication
Reverse insertion order is easiest; imposing an order enables deletion

questions.explanation: It doesn't necessarily matter in which order rows are stored. The alternative is to impose an order, as with SSTables, and use it as an indexing mechanism — sortedness is optional here, and when chosen it doubles as an index.

questions.question: Why can't each column be sorted independently?

options.text: Row reconstruction needs the kth item of each column to be the same row
Because sorting each column separately is computationally too expensive
Because compression algorithms require one global ordering
Because the query optimizer assumes insertion order throughout

questions.explanation: So the data needs to be sorted an entire row at a time, even though it is stored by column. Positional correspondence is the invariant that independent sorting would destroy.

questions.question: Who picks the sort order in a column store, and what are the first and second sort key examples?

options.text: The administrator, from knowledge of the common queries
The query optimizer, automatically, at the time each query runs
The storage engine, based on the measured cardinality of each column
The application developer, separately for every query issued

questions.explanation: If queries often target recent date ranges, date_key first lets the optimizer scan only the last month. A second sort key orders rows sharing the first value, so product_sk groups a day's sales for one product together — helping queries that group or filter by product within a date range.

questions.question: Why does sorting help compression, and how does the effect decay across sort keys?

options.text: Few distinct values give long runs; later sort keys are jumbled
Sorting helps every column equally, since each column file is compressed independently
Sorting actively hurts compression, which is why insertion order is usually preferred
Sorting only improves the compression of numeric columns, not string-valued ones

questions.explanation: A simple run-length encoding could compress the first sort column to a few kilobytes even with billions of rows; columns further down the priority appear in essentially random order. Run-length encoding could compress that column to a few kilobytes even with billions of rows. Columns further down the sorting priority appear in essentially random order. But having the first few columns sorted is still a win overall.

questions.question: Whose idea was storing several different sort orders, and what makes it almost free?

options.text: C-Store, adopted by Vertica; replication already duplicates the data
Bigtable, adopted by HBase; compression makes the extra copies cheap
Dremel, adopted by Parquet; the columnar layout makes copies free
Hive; it is free simply because storage has become inexpensive

questions.explanation: Different queries benefit from different sort orders, and data needs replicating anyway so you don't lose it when a machine fails — so store that redundant data sorted differently and use whichever version fits the query. The redundancy you already pay for is repurposed for performance.

questions.question: Multiple sort orders in a column store are 'a bit similar' to what, and where does the analogy break?

options.text: Multiple secondary indexes; but column stores have no pointers, so each sort order is a full copy
Materialized views; but a view is virtual rather than an actual copy stored on disk
Table partitioning; but partitions are disjoint rather than overlapping copies
Replication; but replicas are byte-identical to one another rather than reordered

questions.explanation: A row-oriented store keeps every row in one place — the heap file or clustered index — and secondary indexes hold only pointers to matching rows. No pointers means each sort order is a complete copy, not a lightweight index.

questions.question: Why do the columnar optimizations make writes difficult? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Update-in-place, as B-trees do, is not possible with compressed columns
Inserting mid-table would mean rewriting every column file consistently
Column files cannot be appended to under any circumstances
Each write requires a distributed transaction across the column files

questions.explanation: Rows are identified by their position within a column, so an insertion has to update all columns consistently. The workload assumption that justifies all of it: most of the load is large read-only queries run by analysts.

questions.question: What solves the columnar write problem, and who does this?

options.text: LSM-trees: writes buffer in memory, then merge into column files in bulk
B-trees paired with a write-ahead log, which is the approach Parquet takes internally
Materialized views refreshed on every write, which is the approach Hive takes
Anti-caching of the coldest columns, which is the approach C-Store introduced

questions.explanation: This is essentially what Vertica does; it doesn't matter whether the in-memory store is row- or column-oriented. It doesn't matter whether the in-memory store is row-oriented or column-oriented; when enough writes accumulate they are merged with the column files and written to new files. The same structure that solved write throughput for OLTP solves it for columnar analytics.

questions.question: With an in-memory write store, what must queries do, and what does the analyst perceive?

options.text: Examine disk columns and memory writes together, hidden by the optimizer
Read only the on-disk columns, leaving recent writes invisible until the next merge
Be re-run by hand once each background merge into the column files has completed
Read the in-memory store for new data only when given an explicit query flag

questions.explanation: Read-your-writes is preserved despite the two-tier storage: inserts, updates and deletes are immediately reflected in subsequent queries.

questions.question: Before introducing materialized aggregates, the chapter makes a concession about columnar storage. What does it concede and claim?

options.text: Not every warehouse is columnar, but columnar can be much faster ad hoc
That columnar storage is consistently slower for ad hoc analytic queries than rows
That every data warehouse in production use today is built as a column store
That row-oriented data warehouses are now entirely obsolete and should be migrated

questions.explanation: Traditional row-oriented databases and a few other architectures are also used. A characteristic move: state the exception before making the general claim.

questions.question: Which SQL aggregate functions does the chapter name, and what is the argument for caching their results?

options.text: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX; recrunching raw data for aggregates many queries share is wasteful
GROUP BY and HAVING; the chapter argues against caching their results entirely
RANK and DENSE_RANK; caching applies only to window functions over partitions
DISTINCT and UNION; caching their results mainly saves network bandwidth

questions.explanation: Repetition across queries is what makes precomputation pay.

questions.question: Define materialized view versus virtual view, and describe what the SQL engine does when you read from each.

options.text: Virtual views expand on the fly; materialized views are a copy on disk
Materialized views are a shortcut for writing queries; virtual views are copies on disk
Both are copies written to disk, differing only in how often each is refreshed
Both are expanded on the fly at query time, differing only in whether results get cached

questions.explanation: A view is a table-like object whose contents are the results of some query. Copy on disk versus expansion at query time is the whole difference: a virtual view is just a shortcut for writing queries.

questions.question: Why must materialized views be maintained, and where do they belong?

options.text: They are denormalized copies, so writes cost more — rarely worth it in OLTP
They need no maintenance at all, since they are recomputed from scratch on every read
They belong in OLTP databases, where writes are cheap and reads are latency-critical
They must be refreshed by hand by whichever analyst originally created the view

questions.explanation: The database can update them automatically. Note the closing hedge — whether they actually improve read performance depends on the individual case.

questions.question: Give both names for the special case of a materialized view, and describe what aggregating along an axis yields.

options.text: Data cube or OLAP cube; aggregating along a row or column gives a summary with one fewer dimension
