Star cube or fact cube; aggregating along an axis adds a further dimension
Snowflake cube or dimension cube; aggregating along an axis returns the raw facts
Hypercube or pivot cube; aggregating along an axis yields a single scalar

questions.explanation: A grid of aggregates grouped by different dimensions. In two dimensions, dates on one axis and products on the other, each cell holding the SUM of net_price for that combination — so a row gives sales by product regardless of date. Figure 3-9's five dimensions (date, product, store, promotion, customer) make a five-dimensional hypercube.

questions.question: State the data cube's advantage and its exact disadvantage, plus the policy most warehouses adopt.

options.text: Precomputed queries fly, but non-dimension attributes cannot be asked about
Cubes save a lot of disk space but query slowly, so they should replace the raw data
Cubes are always perfectly current but need indexes, so index every single dimension
Cubes can answer arbitrary queries but need maintenance, so the raw data is discarded

questions.explanation: For example there is no way to calculate which proportion of sales came from items costing more than $100, because price isn't a dimension — so most warehouses keep as much raw data as possible and use cubes only as a performance boost. Total sales per store yesterday is just a lookup along one dimension, with no need to scan millions of rows. But there is no way to compute what proportion of sales came from items costing more than $100, because price isn't a dimension. Precomputation buys speed by fixing the questions in advance.

questions.question: The Summary splits storage engines in two. Which bottleneck belongs to which?

options.text: OLTP: small key lookups bound by seek time. Analytics: scans bound by bandwidth
OLTP is bound by disk bandwidth, whereas analytics is bound by disk seek time
Both OLTP and analytics turn out to be bound by disk seek time on modern hardware
Both OLTP and analytics are bound by available CPU rather than by the disk at all

questions.explanation: OLTP is user-facing with a huge volume of requests each touching few records by key via an index. Analytics serves business analysts at much lower query volume, but each query scans many millions of records — and column-oriented storage is an increasingly popular solution.

questions.question: Name the two OLTP schools of thought and assign the systems the Summary lists.

options.text: Log-structured, which only appends, and update-in-place, which overwrites pages
Row-oriented and column-oriented, a split that maps onto OLTP and OLAP respectively
In-memory and on-disk schools, split between systems like Redis and PostgreSQL
Hash-index and sorted-index schools, split between Bitcask and B-tree engines

questions.explanation: Log-structured covers Bitcask, SSTables, LSM-trees, LevelDB, Cassandra, HBase and Lucene; B-trees are the biggest update-in-place example, used in all major relational databases and many nonrelational ones. The log-structured school only appends and deletes obsolete files, never updating one already written; the update-in-place school treats the disk as fixed-size pages that can be overwritten, B-trees being the biggest example, used in all major relational databases and many nonrelational ones. Immutability versus overwriting is the deepest division in OLTP storage design.

questions.question: What single idea does the Summary credit log-structured engines with, and why does it matter for hardware?

options.text: Turning random-access writes into sequential writes, raising throughput on both hard drives and SSDs
Eliminating secondary indexes altogether, which greatly reduces memory pressure
Compressing all stored data, which reduces the disk capacity a dataset requires
Avoiding the write-ahead log entirely, which halves the engine's write amplification

questions.explanation: A comparatively recent development. Both media are named — the claim is not restricted to spinning disks, though earlier sections say the advantage is most pronounced there.

questions.question: Why does the Summary say analytics stops caring about indexes?

options.text: Sequential scans make indexes far less relevant; compact encoding matters
Because analytic queries almost always look their rows up by the primary key
Because indexes cannot be built on fact tables, only on the dimension tables
Because materialized views replace indexes entirely in a data warehouse setting

questions.explanation: The aim becomes minimizing the amount of data the query must read from disk, and column-oriented storage helps achieve that goal. The goal shifts from locating rows to minimizing bytes read.

questions.question: What does the chapter claim for you at the end, and what does it disclaim?

options.text: Claims you can pick a tool and reason about tuning; disclaims expertise
Claims you could now implement a storage engine of your own; it disclaims nothing at all
Claims you can now tune any engine expertly; it disclaims only the OLAP material
Claims nothing for you; it disclaims the whole chapter as optional background reading

questions.explanation: You can imagine what effect a higher or lower value may have, and it has hopefully given you enough vocabulary and ideas to make sense of the documentation for the database of your choice — matching the promise made at the start: a rough idea of what the engine is doing under the hood.
